newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia euthanasia pioneer says law should stay.
newsitem.headline: Australia euthanasia pioneer says law should stay.

text.p: The architect of the world's first assisted suicide law urged Australians on Friday to lobby their national politicians to stop them overturning the controversial legislation.

Reacting to the first death under the Northern Territory's "Rights of the Terminally Ill Act", former chief minister Marshall Perron said politicians risked being swayed by a wave of anger over the death.
"The opponents scare politicians, but the supporters do not," Perron told Reuters in this Northern Territory capital.
"I think that the politicians are in fact supportive, but the opponents of euthanasia are so vociferous and the supporters don't have that fanatical look in their eyes," he added.
Bob Dent, a 66-year-old cancer patient, became on Sunday the first person to die under the law pushed through by Perron last year and which came into operation in July.
The death, revealed on Thursday, outraged church leaders and pro-life groups who called for the "shameful" law to be wiped from the books.

A conservative backbencher, backed by Prime Minister John Howard, has launched a private bid in the federal parliament to have Canberra use its constitutional powers to quash the law. That bill is expected to be voted on later this year.
Perron said Dent's death would boost the pro-euthanasia cause, but would also galvanise opponents: "It's a double-edged sword, it's hardened both sides."
He added: "Every Australian should write to their federal members and senators protesting and asking them to back off."
Political leaders, including Howard and his deputy, Tim Fischer, have condemned the law. Fischer said on Thursday it would create a "culture of death" in Australia.
But various opinion polls carried out before Dent's death show strong public support for the idea of voluntary euthanasia, with up to eight in 10 Australians in favour.

Perron, who resigned as chief minister on shepherding through the mercy killing act in May last year, said there was a danger politicians could ignore the level of public backing because euthanasia's backers were not as active as its foes.
